title: Wealth Creation for Expanding the Middle Class in the Philippines
authors: Albert, J.R.G.; Briones, R.M.; Rivera, J.P.R.
tldr: The Philippine middle class grew from 28.5% in 1991 to 39.8% in 2021 but COVID-19 reversed gains, and a four-pronged strategy of climate justice, MSME trade opportunities, workforce readiness, and digital governance is proposed for expansion.
problem_and_motivation: The Philippines aims to become a predominantly middle-class society free of poverty by 2040 but faces significant global headwinds including geopolitical fragmentation, technological disruption, climate change, and widening inequalities that threaten this aspiration. Growing the middle class requires new wealth creation rather than poverty reduction or redistribution alone, yet the country's structural transformation has been slower than other East Asian economies.
approach: Used income-based definition of middle class as households with per capita incomes between 2 to 12 times the official poverty line.
Analyzed data from the 2021 Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES) and July 2021 round of the Labor Force Survey (LFS).
Compared middle-class trends across FIES rounds from 1991, 2006, 2015, 2018, and 2021.
Profiled middle-class characteristics including geography, demographics, education, employment, income sources, expenditure, and assets.
Reviewed international and domestic literature on middle-class drivers including structural transformation, education, urbanization, and globalization.
Proposed a multi-pronged strategy encompassing climate justice, MSME trade and investment, workforce readiness, and digital governance.
findings: num: Middle class grew from 28.5% in 1991 to 39.8% in 2021, representing 34.4 million Filipinos.
num: COVID-19 reversed gains as the middle-class share fell from 43.5% in 2018 to 39.8% in 2021.
num: 60.6% of urban residents are middle-class compared to only 33.8% of rural residents.
num: 40.6% of middle-class Filipinos aged 15+ completed college versus 14.5% of low-income counterparts.
num: 79.5% of employed middle-class individuals hold permanent jobs versus 31.4% of low-income workers with short-term employment.
num: 5.1% of Filipino families have an OFW, and 74.7% of families with OFWs are middle-class.
num: Middle-class unemployment rate is 6.7%, nearly matching the low-income rate of 6.9%.
num: 24.1% of 5-year-olds from middle-income families are not attending school.

Figure 2: Share of Income Clusters by Urban/Rural Area → Urban residents are disproportionately middle-class at 60.6%.

definitions.definition: Family Income and Expenditure Survey, a nationwide survey conducted by PSA collecting household income, expenditure, and socioeconomic data.
Labor Force Survey, a quarterly survey collecting data on employment, unemployment, and labor market indicators.
Overseas Filipino Worker, a Filipino working abroad who remits income to family in the Philippines.
Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprise, comprising 99.5% of all Philippine businesses and employing 63% of the workforce.
Philippine Institute for Development Studies, a state think tank on development policy.
National Capital Region, the metropolitan area of Metro Manila.
Philippine Identification System, a national digital identity system implemented by PSA.
Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises Act, enacted in 2021 to reduce corporate income tax and rationalize fiscal incentives.
Fourth Industrial Revolution, characterized by fusion of digital, physical, and biological technologies.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a comprehensive empirical profile of the Philippine middle class using 2021 FIES and LFS data, documenting its size, growth trajectory, socioeconomic characteristics, and regional variations. It offers a systematic analysis of how income distribution, employment patterns, educational attainment, and asset ownership differ across income classes. The paper contributes a multi-pronged policy framework for middle-class expansion spanning climate justice, MSME development, workforce readiness, and digital governance. It also documents the vulnerability of the middle class to economic shocks, particularly COVID-19, and the role of overseas migration and remittances in income dynamics.
directly_justifies: The Philippine middle class is predominantly urban, more educated, and more engaged in formal employment compared to lower income groups.
The middle class grew from 28.5% in 1991 to 39.8% in 2021 but COVID-19 reversed gains from the 43.5% peak in 2018.
Middle-class unemployment at 6.7% is nearly as high as the low-income class at 6.9%, indicating structural labor market challenges.
40.6% of middle-class Filipinos aged 15 and above completed college compared to only 14.5% of low-income counterparts.
79.5% of employed middle-class individuals hold permanent jobs, indicating formal employment dominance.
limits: Income-based definition does not fully capture the multidimensional nature of middle-class status.
Per capita income approach may not account for household economies of scale or cost-of-living variations across areas.
Analysis relies on cross-sectional FIES data which limits causal inference about middle-class dynamics.
Policy recommendations are broad and lack specific implementation mechanisms or cost estimates. [unacknowledged]
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan was conducted across all 14 topic domains in the taxonomy. The paper was flagged as primarily relevant to Domain 1 (Filipino Demographics and Financial Behavior) because it profiles the socioeconomic characteristics of Filipino households, though it does not focus specifically on young professionals. Domain 2 (Culturally Specific Financial Practices) received low-to-contextual relevance for its coverage of OFW remittances and income sources. Domain 4 (Landscape of Existing Personal Finance Systems) was flagged as contextual because the paper discusses digital financial services and financial inclusion at a policy level. Domain 10 (Data Privacy and Security) received contextual relevance for its coverage of cybersecurity in digital governance. Domains 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, and 14 were considered and rejected as the paper does not address expense categorization, behavioral profiling, predictive modeling, budgeting algorithms, anomaly detection, mobile-first design, engagement mechanics, evaluation frameworks, savings/debt management, or synthetic data generation. The paper is fundamentally a macroeconomic policy document on middle-class expansion rather than a personal finance management systems paper.

limitations: Income-based definition does not capture multidimensional nature of middle-class status beyond income.
Per capita income approach may not account for household economies of scale or cost-of-living variations.
Analysis relies on cross-sectional FIES data limiting causal inference about middle-class dynamics.
Policy recommendations lack specific implementation mechanisms or cost estimates. [unacknowledged]
